reviews.notes: Krishna defines the true sannyāsin and yogin as one who performs duty without reliance on the fruits of action.
Equivalence of sannyāsa and yoga: no one becomes a yogin without renouncing selfish motive and imagination.
Dynamic of spiritual progress: action is the instrument for ascending yoga, while serenity is the mark of attainment.
Definition of the yogārūḍha: one detached from sensory objects and actions, having renounced all selfish schemes.
Classic dictum on self-elevation: let each raise the self by the Self; the Self alone is friend or foe to oneself.
Inner dynamics: the Self is friend to one who has conquered self, but behaves like an enemy to the unconquered.
The self-governed soul in serene peace remains identical in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor.
The yukta yogin satisfied in wisdom and realization, sensing a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as of equal worth.
The highest marks of spiritual equality toward friends, foes, neutrals, arbiters, saints, and sinners alike.
Prescription of meditation in solitary seclusion, constant, self-controlled, rid of yearning and possession.
Preparation of the meditation seat in a clean spot: neither too high nor too low, layered with grass, skin, and cloth.
Concentration of mind upon the One, stilling thoughts and senses on the seat to achieve self-purification.
Physical posture: holding body, neck, and head erect and motionless, gazing steadily at the nose-tip without wandering.
Serene, fearless, firm in the Brahmacharya vow, with mind controlled and dedicated solely to Krishna as supreme goal.
The disciplined yogin constantly harmonizing his soul reaches the peace abiding in God, culminating in Nirvana.
Golden mean in physical discipline: Yoga is ruined by over-eating, absolute fasting, excessive sleep, or over-vigil.
Yoga destroys all sorrow for him who is temperate in eating, recreation, work, sleeping, and waking hours.
Attainment of yukta status when the disciplined mind rests centered in the Soul, detached from all cravings.
Celebrated simile: as a lamp burns steadfast and motionless in a windless place, so rests the yogin controlled mind.
Beginning of definition of Yoga: where the mind rests stilled by practice, beholding the Self by the Self with joy.
Where the soul experiences the transcendent joy beyond sensory reach and never deviates from divine Truth.
Where, possessing this supreme treasure, no other gain seems greater, and gravest sorrow cannot shake the spirit.
Conclusion of sequence: know that severance from union with grief to be true Yoga, to be pursued with tireless resolve.
Casting away all imaginative desires and curbing the sensory flock on all sides by the power of mind.
Attaining quietude step by step through firm intellect, anchoring the mind in the Self and thinking of nothing else.
Restlessness remedy: wherever the wavering mind strays, bring it back under the sovereign control of the Self.
Supreme bliss attends the tranquil-minded yogin whose passion is quieted, who is sinless and one with Brahman.
Constantly uniting the soul to the Supreme, the purified yogin effortlessly tastes the infinite bliss of Brahman.
Equal vision (sama-darśana): the harmonized yogin perceives the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self.
Divine omnipresence: he who sees Me everywhere and all things in Me is never severed from Me nor I from him.
The yogin who, established in unity, adores Me dwelling in all creatures, lives ever in Me whatever his outward state.
Supreme empathy: he who judges the pleasure and pain of all beings by the analogy of his own self is the highest yogin.
Arjuna objection: confesses inability to maintain this steady equanimity owing to the fickle restlessness of the mind.
Arjuna compares the restless, tumultuous, forceful mind to the wild wind, seemingly impossible to bridle.
Krishna concedes the mind is hard to curb, but affirms it can be mastered through persistent practice (abhyāsa) and detachment.
Yoga is elusive for the undisciplined, but accessible to the self-governed seeker who strives with appropriate means.
Arjuna question on the fate of the yoga-bhrashta: what becomes of the believer who falls away from yoga unperfected?
Arjuna asks if such a fallen seeker perishes like a torn cloud, ungrounded and lost to both worlds.
Arjuna asks Krishna to dispel this tormenting doubt completely, since none other can resolve it.
Krishna reassuring promise: neither in this world nor the next does destruction await the doer of good.
The seeker fallen from Yoga dwells in blessed worlds for long ages, then takes birth in a pure and prosperous home.
Or he is born into a family of enlightened yogins, a fortune far rarer and more conducive to spiritual attainment.
In that new birth he recovers the latent spiritual consciousness of his prior life, striving afresh toward perfection.
Carried forward irresistibly by past spiritual momentum, even the mere inquirer surpasses scriptural ritualism.
Striving with earnest perseverance through many lifetimes, the purified yogin at last achieves the supreme goal.
The yogin is exalted above mere ascetics, dry scholars, and ritualistic workers; therefore be a yogin, Arjuna!
Concluding benediction: of all yogins, he who worships Me with inner soul merged in faith is most intimately united.

chapterFindings: Chapter 6 exhibits complete, verse-by-verse one-to-one fidelity for all 47 canonical references.
The practical meditation instructions (6.10-6.15), the four-verse definition of Yoga (6.20-6.23), and the destiny of the fallen seeker (6.37-6.45) align seamlessly with their Sanskrit counterparts.
